nodes.name: angle vector
nodes.statement: Given a compact Riemann surface \(X\) of genus \(g\) with \(n\) distinct points \(P := \{p_1, \ldots, p_n\}\) and an \emph{angle vector} \(\vec{\theta} := (\theta_1, \ldots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}_+^n\) where \(\theta_i \neq 1\), a central question arises: the existence of a singular conformal metric \(g\) of constant curvature \(K \in \{-1, 0, +1\}\) with a conical singularity of angle \(2\pi\theta_i\) at \(p_i\).
nodes.statement_short: Setup: $n$ marked points $P$ on a genus-$g$ surface and an angle vector $\vec\theta$; question of a constant-curvature conical metric with angles $2\pi\theta_i$.

nodes.name: cone hyperbolic, flat, or spherical surface
nodes.statement: A surface equipped with such a metric and constant curvature is referred to as a \textbf{cone hyperbolic, flat}, or \textbf{spherical surface}.

nodes.name: Gauss-Bonnet condition
nodes.statement: The Gauss-Bonnet Formula provides a necessary condition for the existence of such metrics, stipulating that \(2 - 2g + \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_i - 1)\) should share the same signature as \(K\).
conclusions: \(2 - 2g + \sum_{i=1}^n (\theta_i - 1)\) should share the same signature as \(K\)
nodes.statement_short: Necessary condition: $2-2g+\sum(\theta_i-1)$ has the sign of the curvature $K$.

nodes.name: Existence and uniqueness of cone hyperbolic and flat metrics
nodes.statement: For \(K = -1, 0\), this condition is also sufficient, and the metric is unique up to scaling \cite{Heins62, McO88, Tro91}.
conclusions: this condition is also sufficient, and the metric is unique up to scaling

nodes.name: Sufficiency of Gauss-Bonnet for positive genus (Mondello-Panov)
nodes.statement: For \(g > 0\), the Gauss-Bonnet condition is also sufficient \cite{MonPa19}.
conclusions: the Gauss-Bonnet condition is also sufficient

nodes.name: Main theorem: dimension of moduli spaces of dihedral surfaces
nodes.statement: Given an angle vector $\vec{\theta}=(\theta_1, \cdots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}^n_+$ with $\theta_i\neq1$, and $2g-2+n>0$. Assume that all the moduli spaces as follows are non-empty. \begin{enumerate} \item The maximal real dimension of $\mathcal{M}sph^D_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ is $2M_E+M_O+2g-2$, where $M_E$ is the number of integers in $\vec{\theta}$, $M_O$ is the maximal even number not exceeding the number of half-integers in $\vec{\theta}$. \item The real dimension of $\mathcal{M}sph^C_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ is $2M_E+2g-1$ if $(g,n-M_E)\neq(0,0)$, where $M_E$ is the number of integers in $\vec{\theta}$. And the real dimension of $\MsphC{0}{n}{\vec{\theta}}$ is $2n-3$ when $g=0, M_E=n$. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: all the moduli spaces as follows are non-empty
conclusions: The maximal real dimension of $\mathcal{M}sph^D_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ is $2M_E+M_O+2g-2$
The real dimension of $\mathcal{M}sph^C_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ is $2M_E+2g-1$ if $(g,n-M_E)\neq(0,0)$
the real dimension of $\MsphC{0}{n}{\vec{\theta}}$ is $2n-3$ when $g=0, M_E=n$
nodes.statement_short: Strict dihedral moduli space has maximal real dimension $2M_E+M_O+2g-2$; co-axial has $2M_E+2g-1$ (or $2n-3$ for all-integer genus 0).
nodes.label: thm:Main

nodes.name: Non-bubbling condition and the full moduli space
nodes.statement: \textbf{Remark.} Studying the entire moduli space $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ is a much more challenging problem, which currently seems to be beyond our reach. In \cite[Section 6]{MonPa19}, it is asserted that when $\vec{\theta}$ satisfies the so-called “non-bubbling condition”, the real dimension of the moduli space of spherical surfaces with genus $g$ and $n$ prescribed cone angles is precisely $6g - 6 + 2n$. However, this non-bubbling condition seems to be irrelevant to the angle constraint for dihedral surfaces. On one hand, the angle vector for a co-axial surface never satisfies the non-bubbling condition. However, there do exist strict dihedral surfaces whose angle vectors satisfy the non-bubbling condition.
nodes.statement_short: The full moduli space is harder; Mondello-Panov's non-bubbling dimension count $6g-6+2n$ is unrelated to dihedral angle constraints.

nodes.name: Dimension of moduli space under non-bubbling condition (Mondello-Panov)
nodes.statement: In \cite[Section 6]{MonPa19}, it is asserted that when $\vec{\theta}$ satisfies the so-called “non-bubbling condition”, the real dimension of the moduli space of spherical surfaces with genus $g$ and $n$ prescribed cone angles is precisely $6g - 6 + 2n$.
conclusions: the real dimension of the moduli space of spherical surfaces with genus $g$ and $n$ prescribed cone angles is precisely $6g - 6 + 2n$

nodes.name: cone angle
nodes.statement: This indicates that at each point, in geodesic polar coordinates, the metric is locally expressed as \begin{equation*} \mathrm{d}s^2=\left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \mathrm{d}r^2 + \alpha^2 \sinh^2 r \mathrm{d}\theta^2 & , K=-1 & \quad \text{(hyperbolic geometry)} \\ \mathrm{d}r^2 + \alpha^2 r^2 \mathrm{d}\theta^2 & , K=0 & \quad \text{(flat geometry)} \\ \mathrm{d}r^2 + \alpha^2 \sin^2 r \mathrm{d}\theta^2 & , K=+1 & \quad \text{(spherical geometry)} \\ \end{array} \right. \end{equation*} with the cone angle of that point being $2\pi\alpha>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Local polar form of a constant-curvature metric with cone angle $2\pi\alpha$.

nodes.name: cone points
nodes.statement: Here $\alpha\neq1$ only at finitely many isolated points, which we refer to as \emph{cone points}.

nodes.name: unit sphere in spherical coordinates
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{S}^2\subset\mathbb{R}^3$ be the unit sphere, parameterized by spherical coordinates $$ \mathbb{S}^2 = \big\{\ (\psi,\phi):=(\cos\psi\sin\phi, \sin\psi\sin\phi,\cos\phi) \ \big\rvert\ \psi\in[0,2\pi),\ \phi\in[0,\pi]\ \big\} $$ and $N=(0,0), S=(0,\pi)$ be the north and south pole.
nodes.statement_short: Unit sphere parameterized by longitude $\psi$ and colatitude $\phi$, with poles $N,S$.

nodes.name: sector
nodes.statement: Given $\alpha\in(0,1)$ and $r\in(0,\pi]$, \[ \textcolor{black}{B_\alpha(r)} :=\big\{\ (\psi,\phi) \ \rvert\ \psi\in[0,2\pi\alpha],\ \phi\in[0,r)\ \big\} \] is called a \emph{sector} of angle $2\pi\alpha$ centered at $N$ with radius $r$.

nodes.name: topological sector $B_\theta(r)$
nodes.statement: For any $\theta>0$, let $M$ be the smallest positive integer such that $\theta/M<1$. We take $M$ copies of $B_{\theta/M}(r)$, denoted by $B^{(i)}$ with vertices $N^{(i)}, P^{(i)}, Q^{(i)}$, $i=1,\cdots, M$. Now gluing the pair of radii $N^{(i-1)}Q^{(i-1)}$ and $N^{(i)}P^{(i)}$ by the $\phi$ parameter for each $i=\textcolor{black}{2},\cdots, M$, we obtain a topological sector denoted by \textcolor{black}{$B_{\theta}(r)$}, and obviously generalizing the previous one.
nodes.statement_short: Glue $M$ small sectors along radii to get a sector of arbitrary angle $2\pi\theta$.

nodes.name: cone $S_\theta(r)$
nodes.statement: If the remained two boundary radii $N^{(M)}Q^{(M)}, N^{(1)}P^{(1)}$ are further glued, we obtain a \emph{cone} of angle $2\pi\theta$ with radius $r$, denoted by \textcolor{black}{$S_\theta(r)$}.

nodes.name: cone spherical surface
nodes.statement: Then we can consider a cone spherical surface\ as a compact metric surface such that every point has a neighborhood isometric to some $S_{\theta}(r)$, with $\theta=\theta_i$ at cone point $p_i$ and $\theta=1$ otherwise.
differentia: every point has a neighborhood isometric to some $S_{\theta}(r)$

nodes.name: spherical bigon
nodes.statement: When $r=\pi$, the closure $\textcolor{black}{B_\theta}:=\overline{B_\theta(\pi)}$ is called a spherical \emph{bigon} of angle $2\pi\theta$, or a bigon of width $\theta$ (see Section \ref{sec:strip_decomp}).

nodes.name: football
nodes.statement: $\textcolor{black}{S_\theta}:=\overline{S_\theta(\pi)}$ is called a \emph{football} of angle $2\pi\theta$.

nodes.name: PSU(2) as isometry group of the sphere
nodes.statement: The isometry group $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ of the unit sphere is identified with $$ \mathrm{PSU}(2)=\left\{\ z\mapsto \frac{az+b}{-\bar{b}z+\bar{a}} \ \bigg\rvert\ a,b\in\mathbb{C}, \abs{a}^2+\abs{b}^2=1 \ \right\} \big{/} \pm I \subset \mathrm{PGL}(2,\mathbb{C}) $$ which acts on the Riemann sphere.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface

nodes.name: standard spherical metric $g_{FS}$
nodes.statement: The standard spherical metric on the Riemann sphere is given by $g_{\rm FS} = 4\lvert \mathrm{d}w \rvert ^2/(1+\lvert w \rvert ^2)^2$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface

nodes.name: developing map
nodes.statement: There exists a multi-valued meromorphic function $D$ on $\Sigma$, branched at the cone points in $P$. Furthermore, the pullback metric $D^*(g_{\rm FS})$ of $g_{\rm FS}$ is coincident with the cone spherical metric\ on $\Sigma$. Such a map $D$ is called a \emph{developing map}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface
differentia: the pullback metric $D^*(g_{\rm FS})$ of $g_{\rm FS}$ is coincident with the cone spherical metric\ on $\Sigma$

nodes.name: monodromy representation and monodromy group
nodes.statement: It has monodromy in $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$. This means that with a base point $z_0\in \Sigma- P$, for any closed curve $\gamma\subset\Sigma- P$ passing through $z_0$, the analytic continuation $D(\gamma\cdot z)$ of $D$ along $\gamma$ can be expressed as $D(\gamma\cdot z) = \rho_D(\gamma)\big( D(z) \big)$, where $\rho_D(\gamma)\in\mathrm{PSU}(2)$. The element $\rho_D(\gamma)$ depends only on the homotopy class of $\gamma$. Consequently, a developing map $D$ induces a \emph{monodromy representation} $\rho_D:\pi_1(\Sigma-P,z_0) \to \mathrm{PSU}(2)$ and its image is called \emph{monodromy group}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface
nodes.statement_short: Analytic continuation of $D$ along loops acts by $\rho_D(\gamma)\in PSU(2)$, giving the monodromy representation and its image group.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of developing map up to PSU(2)
nodes.statement: The developing map is an orientation preserving local isometry, unique up to post-composing by an element of $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$. Similarly, the monodromy representation and group are unique up to conjugation by an element in $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface
conclusions: The developing map is an orientation preserving local isometry, unique up to post-composing by an element of $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$

nodes.name: universal cover of punctured surface
nodes.statement: Let $\pi:\tilde{\Sigma}' \to \Sigma -P$ be the universal cover of the punctured surface $\Sigma -P$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface

nodes.name: metric completion $\hat\Sigma$ and extended developing map
nodes.statement: This map extends to the metric completion $\hat{\Sigma}$ of $\tilde{\Sigma}'$, which we continue to call a developing map and denote it by $D$.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface

nodes.name: notation $\rho(\pi_1)$
nodes.statement: We shall denote the monodromy group by $\rho(\pi_1)$ in short.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface

nodes.name: co-axial cone spherical surface
nodes.statement: A cone spherical surface\ is called \emph{co-axial} if its monodromy group fixes an axis of ${\Bbb S}^2$. In other words, $\rho(\pi_1)$ is conjugated to a subgroup of $$ \mathrm{U}(1) := \left\{\ z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}z = \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta/2}z}{\mathrm{e}^{-\mathbf{i}\theta/2}} \ \bigg\rvert\ \theta\in\mathbb{R} \ \right\} \cong \mathrm{SO}(2). $$ This concept is equivalent to \emph{reducible metric} in \cite{UYa00}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface
differentia: its monodromy group fixes an axis of ${\Bbb S}^2$
nodes.label: def:coaxial

nodes.name: dihedral and strict dihedral surface
nodes.statement: A cone spherical surface\ is called \emph{dihedral} if its monodromy group preserves a pair of antipodal points on the unit sphere ${\Bbb S}^2$. Equivalently, $\rho(\pi_1)$ is conjugated to a subgroup of $$ \mathrm{O}(2) := \left\{\ z\mapsto \mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}z,\ z\mapsto \frac{\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}}{z} \ \bigg\rvert\ \theta\in\mathbb{R} \ \right\} \cong \mathbb{Z}_2 \ltimes \mathrm{U}(1). $$ A dihedral surface that is not co-axial is called \emph{strict dihedral}.
nodes.section: 2.2 Developing map, monodromy and dihedral surface
nodes.origin_citation: Song, Cheng, Li & Xu 2020; Gendron & Tahar 2023
differentia: its monodromy group preserves a pair of antipodal points on the unit sphere ${\Bbb S}^2$
nodes.label: def:dihedral

nodes.name: abelian differential
nodes.statement: A meromorphic \emph{abelian differential}, denoted as $\omega$, is a meromorphic 1-form on $X$.

nodes.name: quadratic differential
nodes.statement: A meromorphic \emph{quadratic differential}, denoted as $q$, is a meromorphic section of $K_X^{\otimes 2}$.

nodes.name: critical and regular points of a differential
nodes.statement: The zeros and poles of a differential are called the \emph{critical points}, while all other points are \emph{regular points}.

nodes.name: primitive quadratic differential
nodes.statement: We call a quadratic differential\ \emph{primitive} if it is not the square of an abelian differential globally.
differentia: it is not the square of an abelian differential globally

nodes.name: Real-period criterion for dihedral metrics
nodes.statement: Conversely, a meromorphic quadratic differential\ $q$ induces a dihedral cone spherical metric\ if and only if the integral of $\sqrt{q}$ is real along any closed curve on $\Sigma-P$ and for any choice of analytic branch of the square root \cite{Li19,SCLX20}.
conclusions: a meromorphic quadratic differential\ $q$ induces a dihedral cone spherical metric\ if and only if the integral of $\sqrt{q}$ is real along any closed curve on $\Sigma-P$ and for any choice of analytic branch of the square root
equivalent_conditions: a meromorphic quadratic differential\ $q$ induces a dihedral cone spherical metric
the integral of $\sqrt{q}$ is real along any closed curve on $\Sigma-P$ and for any choice of analytic branch of the square root
nodes.statement_short: A quadratic differential induces a dihedral metric iff all periods of $\sqrt q$ are real.

nodes.name: foliation
nodes.statement: A \emph{foliation} on a surface is a decomposition of the 2-dimensional surface into 1-dimensional immersed manifolds.

nodes.name: singularities of a foliation
nodes.statement: There may be isolated points, called \emph{singularities}, where this decomposition is not well-defined.

nodes.name: leaves
nodes.statement: The 1-dimensional manifolds, or the trajectories of the line field, are called \emph{leaves}.

nodes.name: singular and regular leaves
nodes.statement: Leaves that meet singularities are called \emph{singular leaves}, while those without any singularity are called \emph{regular leaves}.

nodes.name: orientable foliation
nodes.statement: A foliation is \emph{orientable} if it possesses a globally continuous orientation for all its leaves outside singularities.
differentia: it possesses a globally continuous orientation for all its leaves outside singularities

nodes.name: index of a singularity
nodes.statement: For convenience, the \emph{index} $\textcolor{black}{\mathrm{Ind}(p)}$ of a singularity $p$ of a foliation here is defined as twice the index specified in \cite{Hopf83}.

nodes.name: $s$-prong singularity
nodes.statement: In particular, when $\mathrm{Ind}(p)\leq1$, $p$ is an \emph{$s$-prong}, where $s=2-\mathrm{Ind}(p)$ denotes the number of leaf segments converging at that singularity.

nodes.name: Poincaré-Hopf Theorem
nodes.statement: Suppose $F$ is a foliation on a closed surface $S$ of genus $g\geq0$. Then \begin{equation} \sum_{\mathrm{singularities}\ p} \mathrm{Ind}(p) = 2 (2- 2g). \end{equation}
assumptions: $F$ is a foliation on a closed surface $S$ of genus $g\geq0$
conclusions: \sum_{\mathrm{singularities}\ p} \mathrm{Ind}(p) = 2 (2- 2g).
nodes.statement_short: Sum of (doubled) singularity indices of a foliation equals $2(2-2g)$.
nodes.label: thm:PH

nodes.name: Poincaré-Hopf index formula
nodes.statement: \sum_{\mathrm{singularities}\ p} \mathrm{Ind}(p) = 2 (2- 2g).
nodes.label: eq:PH

nodes.name: measured foliation
nodes.statement: A \emph{measured foliation} on a closed surface $S$ is a foliation with a transverse measure that assigns each transverse arc a positive measure.
differentia: with a transverse measure that assigns each transverse arc a positive measure

nodes.name: pair of transverse measured foliations of a quadratic differential
nodes.statement: Each quadratic differential\ $q$ on a Riemann surface $X$ gives rise to a pair of transverse measured foliation s $(H_q, V_q)$. This means that $H_q, V_q$ share the same set of singularities and their respective indexes match. Moreover, outside the singularities, the leaves of $H_q$ and $V_q$ intersect transversely.

nodes.name: horizontal foliation $H_q$
nodes.statement: A horizontal trajectory of $q$ corresponds to a horizontal line with constant $y$-coordinate. All these horizontal trajectories form the horizontal foliation $H_q$. The transverse measure on a transverse arc of $H_q$ is the total variation of $y$-coordinate, given by $\abs{\mathrm{d}y}=\abs{\mathrm{Im}\sqrt{q}}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $q=dz^2$ on $\mathbb C$, horizontal lines form $H_q$, with transverse measure $|dy|$.

nodes.name: vertical foliation $V_q$
nodes.statement: The vertical foliation $V_q$ is defined similarly, with the $y$-coordinate replaced by the $x$-coordinate.

nodes.name: Index of a critical point of a quadratic differential
nodes.statement: At a critical point $z_0$ of $q$, there exists a coordinate chart such that $z_0$ is mapped to $0$ and locally $q=c z^k\mathrm{d}z^2$, where $c\in\mathbb{C}^*$ is constant and $k\geq-2$. Then $z_0$ is a singularity of index $(2-k)$ for both foliations.
assumptions: locally $q=c z^k\mathrm{d}z^2$, where $c\in\mathbb{C}^*$ is constant and $k\geq-2$
conclusions: $z_0$ is a singularity of index $(2-k)$ for both foliations

nodes.name: Strebel differentials induce dihedral metrics
nodes.statement: \textbf{Remark.} Strebel differential, whose regular leaves of $V_q$ are all closed curves around exactly one pole, is a special type of differentials that induces dihedral metrics. They correspond to hemispherical surfaces in \cite[Section 2.5]{GT23}, and are related to limit surfaces of grafting along a multicurve \cite[Section 5.2]{Gup14}.

nodes.name: latitude and longitude foliations on the sphere
nodes.statement: There is a natural pair of transverse measured foliations on $\mathbb{S}^2$. \begin{itemize} \item The \emph{latitude foliation} \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{F}$} consists of all latitude circles of $\mathbb{S}^2$. The measure of a transverse arc is given by the total variation of latitude. \item The \emph{longitude foliation} \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{G}$} consists of all meridian lines of $\mathbb{S}^2$. The measure of a transverse arc is given by the total variation of longitude. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: On $\mathbb S^2$: latitude circles with latitude-variation measure, and meridians with longitude-variation measure.
nodes.label: def:LL_foli_sphere

nodes.name: conformal Mercator map
nodes.statement: Consider the \emph{conformal Mercator map} $Mer:\mathbb{C} \to \mathbb{S}^2-\{N,S\}$ given by \begin{equation} Z=\psi+\mathbf{i} Y \longmapsto \left( \psi, 2\arctan(\mathrm{e}^Y) \right). \end{equation}

nodes.name: Mercator map formula
nodes.statement: Z=\psi+\mathbf{i} Y \longmapsto \left( \psi, 2\arctan(\mathrm{e}^Y) \right).

nodes.name: Mercator map in complex coordinate
nodes.statement: Z = \psi+\mathbf{i} Y \longmapsto \exp(\mathbf{i} Z) = \mathrm{e}^{-Y}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\psi}.

nodes.name: Argument for O(2)-invariance of the latitude/longitude foliations
nodes.statement: It can be observed that the differentials $\mathrm{d}\theta$ and $2\mathrm{d}r/(1+r^2)$ are fixed by $\mathrm{U}(1)$-action, and remain invariant up to signature under $\mathrm{O}(2)$-action.
nodes.statement_short: Direct check: $d\theta$ and $2dr/(1+r^2)$ are $U(1)$-fixed and $O(2)$-invariant up to sign.

nodes.name: Latitude and longitude foliations are O(2)-invariant
nodes.statement: Therefore, as measured foliation s, the latitude foliation $\mathcal{F}$ and the longitude foliation $\mathcal{G}$ are both fixed by the $\mathrm{O}(2)$-action.
conclusions: the latitude foliation $\mathcal{F}$ and the longitude foliation $\mathcal{G}$ are both fixed by the $\mathrm{O}(2)$-action

nodes.name: latitude and longitude foliation; foliated dihedral surface
nodes.statement: Let $\Sigma$ be a dihedral cone spherical surface. \begin{enumerate} \item Let $D$ be a developing map such that $\rho(\pi_1)\subset \mathrm{O}(2)$. Then $\textcolor{black}{F}:=\pi_* D^*(\mathcal{F})$ and $\textcolor{black}{G}:=\pi_* D^*(\mathcal{G})$ are well-defined measured foliation s on $\Sigma$. $F$ and $G$ are also called \emph{latitude and longitude foliation} of $\Sigma$ with respect to $D$, regarded as horizontal and vertical foliation. \item $\Sigma$ together with a pair of latitude and longitude foliation $(F,G)$ is called a \emph{foliated (dihedral) surface}, denoted by a triple \textcolor{black}{$(\Sigma;F,G)$}. \end{enumerate}
also_stated_at: A dihedral surface together with a pair of foliations is called a foliated surface (Definition \ref{def:LL_foli}).
nodes.statement_short: Pull back the sphere's latitude/longitude foliations by an $O(2)$-equivariant developing map; a surface with such a pair is a foliated surface.
nodes.label: def:LL_foli

nodes.name: absolute latitude function
nodes.statement: So for any dihedral surface $\Sigma$ with developing map $D$ as above, $\abs{\cos\phi}$ can induce a function $H:\Sigma\to[0,1]$, called the \emph{absolute latitude function}.

nodes.name: equatorial net, poles and zeroes of the foliations
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{enumerate} \item The set $\pi (D^{-1} \{\phi=\frac\pi2\}) \subset \Sigma$ is called the \emph{equatorial net} of the foliated surface or both foliations $F,G$, denoted by \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{E}$}. \item Points in $\textcolor{black}{Q}:=\pi (D^{-1}\{N,S\}) $ are called the \emph{poles} of both foliations. This is the set of singularities with index $+2$. \item Other singularities are called the \emph{zeroes} of both foliations, with all indexes $\leq +1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Equatorial net = preimage of the equator; poles = preimages of $N,S$ (index $+2$); other singularities are zeroes.
nodes.label: def:singular_info

nodes.name: Argument on cone angles at singularities
nodes.statement: By the geometry of $\mathrm{O}(2)$ actions on $\mathbb{S}^2$, the cone angle depends on the position of a cone point. As discussed in Section \ref{sec:dihedral}, the monodromy representation of a simple loop surrounding a cone point $p\in P$ is a rotation. One of the fixed points of this rotation is the developing map image of the point in $\hat{\Sigma} - \tilde{\Sigma}'$ corresponding to the loop. When $p$ lies on the equatorial net, the developing map image of the point lies on the equator of $\mathbb{S}^2$. Since $\mathrm{O}(2)$ action preserves the equator, the representation of the simple loop must either be trivial or a $\pi$-rotation. And consequently, the cone angle of $p$ is an integer multiple of $\pi$. When $p$ is a pole of the foliations, the representation of the simple loop can be an arbitrary rotation that fixes the two poles. Finally, if $p$ is not a pole or a point on the equatorial net, the representation of the simple loop must be trivial and the cone angle is an integer multiple of $2\pi$. For a co-axial surface, if $p$ is not a pole, its cone angle must be an integer multiple of $2\pi$, since $\pi$-rotation about a point on the equator is not allowed.
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the position of a cone point (equatorial net, pole, elsewhere) and the corresponding monodromy rotation.

nodes.name: Cone points are singularities of the foliations
nodes.statement: So every cone point must be a singularity of the foliations, but a pole singularity may be a smooth point of the metric.
conclusions: every cone point must be a singularity of the foliations
a pole singularity may be a smooth point of the metric

nodes.name: intersection number $i(F,\gamma)$
nodes.statement: An embedded regular leaf segment $\gamma:[0,1]\to\Sigma$ of $G$ is a geodesic arc. The \emph{total measure} of $\gamma$ under $F$, also referred to as the \emph{intersection number} of $F$ and $\gamma$, is defined as the spherical length of $\gamma$, denoted by $i(F,\gamma)$.

nodes.name: intersection number $i(G,\delta)$
nodes.statement: Similarly, consider another embedded regular leaf segment $\delta:[0,1]\to\Sigma$ of $F$. Let $\tilde{\delta}$ be a lifting of $\delta$ through the covering $\pi:\hat{\Sigma}\to\Sigma$. The total measure of $\delta$ under $G$, or the intersection number $i(G,\delta)$, is defined as the total longitude variation of $D({\tilde{\delta}})$ on $\mathbb{S}^2$.

nodes.name: Measure of a closed latitude leaf around a pole equals the cone angle
nodes.statement: In particular, when $\delta$ is a closed leaf of $F$ surrounding a pole $q$, $i(G,\delta)$ is equal to the cone angle $2\pi\theta_i$ if $q=p_i\in P$, and equal to $2\pi$ if $q\notin P$.
assumptions: $\delta$ is a closed leaf of $F$ surrounding a pole $q$
conclusions: $i(G,\delta)$ is equal to the cone angle $2\pi\theta_i$ if $q=p_i\in P$, and equal to $2\pi$ if $q\notin P$

nodes.name: angle vector (restated)
nodes.statement: As before, let $\vec{\theta}:=(\theta_1, \cdots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}_+^N$ be an angle vector with $\theta_i\neq 1$.

nodes.name: labeled surface and labeled moduli space
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{enumerate} \item A \emph{labeled surface} is a cone spherical surface\ whose cone points are labeled as $p_1,\cdots,p_n$ such that $p_i$ has cone angle of $2\pi \theta_i$, for $i=1,\cdots,n$. \item Let $\Sigma_k\ (k=1,2)$ be two labeled cone spherical surface s, with cone points labeled as $p^k_i, i=1,\cdots,n$. They are \emph{equivalent with label} if there exists an orientation-preserving isometry $I:\Sigma_1 \to \Sigma_2$ such that $I(p^1_i)=p^2_i$ for all $i$. \item The \emph{labeled moduli space} \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$} is all equivalence classes of genus $g$ labeled surfaces with the given angle vector $\vec{\theta}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Cone points carry labels with prescribed angles; label-preserving isometry classes of genus-$g$ surfaces form $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec\theta)$.
nodes.label: def:labeled

nodes.name: Surfaces are labeled
nodes.statement: From now on, all cone spherical surface s with prescribed cone angles will be treated as labeled surfaces.

nodes.name: type partition
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{\theta}=(\theta_1, \cdots, \theta_n) \in \mathbb{R}_+^N$ be an angle vector with $\theta_i\neq 1$. A \emph{(topological) type partition} is a partition $\textcolor{black}{\vec{T}}=( E, O, N )$ of $\{1,\cdots,n\}$ satisfying that \begin{itemize} \item $\forall i\in E, \theta_{i}\in \mathbb{Z}_{>1}$; \item $\forall j\in O, \theta_{j}\in \frac12 + \mathbb{Z}$. \end{itemize} Let $ \#E=n_E, \#O=n_O, \#N=n_N $, then $n_E + n_O + n_N = n$. A foliated surface $(\Sigma;F,G)$ is \emph{of type partition $\vec{T}$}, if $p_i$ is a zero with index $(2-2\theta_i)$ for all $i \in E \cup O$, and $p_k$ is a pole for all $k \in N$.
nodes.statement_short: Partition $(E,O,N)$ of cone points into even-index zeros (integer angles), odd-index zeros (half-integer angles) and poles.

nodes.name: moduli spaces of strict dihedral surfaces
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{T}$ be a type partition as above. \begin{enumerate} \item The moduli space \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{M}sph^D_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$} is the set of all equivalent classes of \textcolor{black}{strict dihedral} cone spherical surface s in $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$. \item \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta})$} is the set of all foliated strict dihedral surfaces $(\Sigma;F,G)$ with $\Sigma\in\mathcal{M}sph^D_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$. \item $\textcolor{black}{\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})} \subset \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta})$ is the set of foliated strict dihedral surfaces of type partition $\vec{T}$. \item $\textcolor{black}{\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})} :=\{ \Sigma \ \lvert\ (\Sigma;F,G)\in \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \}$ is the set of all equivalent classes of (unfoliated) strict dihedral surfaces of type partition $\vec{T}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Moduli of strict dihedral surfaces, of foliated ones, and their restrictions to a type partition $\vec T$.
nodes.label: def:moduli_D

nodes.name: Diagram of strict dihedral moduli spaces
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} \xymatrix{ \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\quad\iota_F} \ar@{->>}[d]^{p_T} & \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta}) \ar@{->>}[d]^{p} &\\ \mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\quad\iota_T} & \mathcal{M}sph^D_{g,n}(\vec{\theta}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\iota} & \mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta}) } \end{gathered}
nodes.label: eq:moduli_spaces_D

nodes.name: No odd zeros for co-axial surfaces
nodes.statement: So we always assume $O=\emptyset$ in the type partition for co-axial surfaces.

nodes.name: moduli spaces of co-axial surfaces
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{enumerate} \item \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{M}sph^C_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$} is the set of all equivalent classes of co-axial cone spherical surface s in $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$. \item \textcolor{black}{$\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta})$} is the set of all foliated co-axial surfaces $(\Sigma;F,G)$ with $\Sigma\in\mathcal{M}sph^C_{g,n}(\vec{\theta})$ and \textcolor{black}{$(F,G)$ orientable measured foliation s}. \item $\textcolor{black}{\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})}\subset \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta})$ is the set of all foliated co-axial surfaces of type partition $\vec{T}$. \item $\textcolor{black}{\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})} :=\{ \Sigma \ \lvert\ (\Sigma;F,G)\in \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \}$ is the set of all (unfoliated) co-axial surfaces of type partition $\vec{T}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Moduli of co-axial surfaces, of those foliated by orientable $(F,G)$, and restrictions to a type partition.
nodes.label: def:moduli_C

nodes.name: Diagram of co-axial moduli spaces
nodes.statement: \begin{gathered} \xymatrix{ \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\quad\iota_F} \ar@{->>}[d]^{p_T} & \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta}) \ar@{->>}[d]^{p} &\\ \mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\quad\iota_T} & \mathcal{M}sph^C_{g,n}(\vec{\theta}) \ar@{^(->}[r]^{\iota} & \mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}(\vec{\theta}) } \end{gathered}
nodes.label: eq:moduli_spaces_C

nodes.name: critical leaves of $G$
nodes.statement: The set of \emph{critical leaves} of $G$, denoted by \textcolor{black}{$\mathrm{Crit}(G)$}, is defined as the union of all leaves of $G$ starting from $P-Q$, which are the zeros of the foliation.
nodes.label: def:Sing_G

nodes.name: Non-critical longitude leaves are geodesics of length pi
nodes.statement: For a foliated surface $(\Sigma;F,G)$, all leaves in $G-\mathrm{Crit}(G)$ are geodesic segments of length $\pi$, ending at points in $Q$.
conclusions: all leaves in $G-\mathrm{Crit}(G)$ are geodesic segments of length $\pi$, ending at points in $Q$
nodes.label: lem:Sing_G

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.2
nodes.statement: All leaves of $\mathcal{G}$ on $\mathbb{S}^2$ are geodesics of length $\pi$, and the developing map $D$ is locally isometric. So every leaf of $G$ on $\Sigma$ must meet a pole within length $\pi$, or stop at a zero before meeting a pole. If a leaf never hits a zero, the developing map along any lifting of this leaf is an isometric immersion. So it is isometric to a leaf of $\mathcal{G}$. This also shows that there is no recurrent leaf in $G$.
nodes.statement_short: Developing map is a local isometry onto $\mathcal G$, whose leaves are geodesics of length $\pi$ between poles.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic-type (g,n) by default
nodes.statement: Unless stated otherwise, we will assume that $2g-2+n>0$ by default.

nodes.name: strip decomposition
nodes.statement: Given a foliated surface $(\Sigma;F,G)$, the critical leaves $\mathrm{Crit}(G)$ partition the surface into a finite number of bigons. This partition is called the \emph{strip decomposition} of $(\Sigma;F,G)$.
nodes.label: def:strip_decomp

nodes.name: marked point of a bigon
nodes.statement: A boundary point of a bigon, other than the two vertices, that is glued to a cone point is considered as a \emph{marked point} of the closed bigon before gluing.

nodes.name: width of a bigon
nodes.statement: The \emph{angle} or the \emph{width} $w_i$ of a bigon $B_i=B_{w_i}$ (see Section \ref{sec:spherical_cone}) in the strip decomposition equals to intersection number $i(G,\alpha)$, where $\alpha$ is a leaf segment of $F$ inside $B_i$ connecting its two boundaries. This quantity is also denoted as $i(G, B_i)$.

nodes.name: gluing pattern
nodes.statement: The number of bigons, the division of the boundaries of the bigons, and the pairing of boundary segments are called the \emph{gluing pattern} of the strip decomposition.

nodes.name: Strip decomposition determines a dihedral surface
nodes.statement: The strip decomposition provides a complete determination for a dihedral surface. Specifically, two dihedral surfaces $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2$ are isometric if and only if there exist corresponding foliated surfaces $(\Sigma_i;F_i,G_i), i=1,2$, such that their strip decompositions are identical. This means that they have the same gluing pattern, bigon widths and position of boundary marked points. In other words, the equivalence holds if and only if there exists a homeomorphism\ $I:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$ such that $I^*(F_2)=F_1, I^*(G_2)=G_1$ as measured foliation s. \hfill $\square$
conclusions: two dihedral surfaces $\Sigma_1, \Sigma_2$ are isometric if and only if there exist corresponding foliated surfaces $(\Sigma_i;F_i,G_i), i=1,2$, such that their strip decompositions are identical
equivalent_conditions: there exist corresponding foliated surfaces $(\Sigma_i;F_i,G_i), i=1,2$, such that their strip decompositions are identical
nodes.statement_short: Two dihedral surfaces are isometric iff they admit foliations with identical strip decompositions.

nodes.name: Three-cone sphere with two strip decompositions
nodes.statement: The strip decomposition in Figure \ref{fig:exp_strip_1}, consisting of three bigons of width $\pi$ (equivalent to hemispheres), gives a surface in $\MsphC{0}{3}{\frac12,\frac12,3}$. The foliated surface belongs to $\MsphCFT{0}{3}{(\frac12,\frac12,3)}{\vec{T}}$ where $\vec{T}=( \{p_3\}, \emptyset, \{p_1, p_2\} )$. This foliation contains two extra poles $q_1, q_2$. \begin{figure}[!h] \centering \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{fig/example_a.png} \caption{A strip decomposition of a surface in $\MsphC{0}{3}{\frac12,\frac12,3}$ into three hemispheres. The boundary segments labeled with the same number are glued in pair. The lengths of boundary segments of label $1,3,5$ are the same.} \end{figure} However, there exits another continuous family of strip decomposition induced by non-orientable foliations. The new poles $q'_1,q'_2,q'_3$ lie on the equatorial net of the previous foliation and are smooth points of the metric. Their positions on the hemispheres are exactly the same. The type partition $\vec{T}'= ( \{p_3\}, \{p_1,p_2\}, \emptyset ) $. The bigons have width of $\theta, 2\pi-2\theta, 2\theta, \pi-\theta$ where $0<\theta<\pi$. \begin{figure}[ht] \centering \includegraphics[width=0.9\textwidth]{fig/example_b.png} \caption{A strip decomposition of the same surface in Figure \ref{fig:exp_strip_1} into four bigons. Two marked points $p_1\in\partial B_1, p_2\in\partial B_4$ are the midpoints. And the lengths of boundary segments of label $3',5',7'$ are the same.} \end{figure} In both figures, the critical leaves of the first and second longitude foliation are represented by the segments in black and blue respectively. The representation of singularities follows the figure legend in Table \ref{tab:singularity}. The monodromy groups of the two foliated surfaces are $\rho_1(\pi_1)=\{\mathrm{id}, z\mapsto -z\}$ and $\rho_2(\pi_1)=\{\mathrm{id}, z\mapsto 1/z\}$. \hfill $\square$
nodes.statement_short: A co-axial sphere with angles $(1/2,1/2,3)$ admits strip decompositions from both orientable and non-orientable foliations.
nodes.label: eg:three_cone_sphere

nodes.name: Consequences of the three-cone-sphere example
nodes.statement: \textbf{Remark.} This example highlights three important facts: \textbf{(1).} The orientation requirement in Definition \ref{def:moduli_C}.(2) is necessary. Without such condition, a foliated co-axial surface could potentially be misclassified as a strict dihedral one. Furthermore, the fiber of $p$ in (\ref{eq:moduli_spaces_C}) over such a surface might contain a component with misleading extra dimension. \textbf{(2).} The existence of a primitive quadratic differential\ does not guarantee a strict dihedral metric. It only indicates that the current developing map induces a primitive differential, but this may not hold for all possible developing maps. The monodromy group is the truly essential quantity. \textbf{(3).} On the same Riemann surface, it is possible to have both an abelian and a primitive quadratic differential\ with the same set of zeros and all real periods. However, the poles of these differentials may be distinct.
nodes.statement_short: The orientation requirement is needed; primitive differentials do not imply strict dihedral; abelian and primitive quadratic differentials can coexist.

nodes.name: critical leaves of $F$
nodes.statement: The set of critical leaves of $F$, denoted by $\mathrm{Crit}(F)$, is defined as the union of all points in $Q$ and leaves of $F$ starting from $P-Q$.

nodes.name: Non-critical latitude leaves are closed
nodes.statement: All leaves in $F-\mathrm{Crit}(F)$ are closed regular leaves. The leaves in the same connected component of $F-\mathrm{Crit}(F)$ are all homotopic.
conclusions: All leaves in $F-\mathrm{Crit}(F)$ are closed regular leaves

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.8
nodes.statement: We can regard the leaves of $F$ as the level set of the Morse function $H^2:\Sigma\to[0,1]$, where $H$ is the absolute latitude foliation defined in Section \ref{sec:ll_foli}. The singularities of $F$ are the critical points of function $H^2$. Then every level set is a closed compact subset of $\Sigma$. Each connected component is a codimension 1 submanifold when it does not contain a critical point. By compactness, it must be a circle. For a connected component $A$ of $F-\mathrm{Crit}(F)$, the restriction of $H^2$ on $A$ is a Morse function with circle fibers over its image. If $0$ is not in the image, then $A$ is a circle bundle over an interval, hence an annulus. If $0$ is in the image, then the preimage circle of $0$ cut $A$ into two annulus in the previous. Since there is no singularity, $A$ is glued from two annuli along one-side boundary, hence an annulus again. This result can also be proved by the strip decomposition. Each leave from a zero of $F$ must end at a zero with the same absolute latitude, because the whole level set is compact. By drawing all these leaves in $F$, each bigon is further divided into rectangles bounded by a pair of geodesic leaf segments in $G$ and a pair of leaf segments in $F$ (the later one may degenerate to a pole point). All remained leaves of $F$ are regular and closed. So gluing these pieces along the segments of $G$, one must obtain punctured disks and annuli.
nodes.statement_short: Leaves of $F$ are level sets of the Morse function $H^2$; regular components are circle bundles over intervals, hence annuli.

nodes.name: annulus decomposition
nodes.statement: Given a foliated surface $(\Sigma;F,G)$, the critical leaves $\mathrm{Crit}(F)$ partition the surface into a finite number of annuli and punctured disks. This partition is called the \emph{annulus decomposition} of $(\Sigma;F,G)$.
nodes.label: def:ann_decomp

nodes.name: height of an annulus
nodes.statement: For a component $A_j$ of the annulus decomposition, the total latitude variation $h_j$ is defined as its \emph{height}. It equals to intersection number $i(F,\beta)$, where $\beta$ is any leaf segment of $G$ inside $B_i$ connecting its two boundaries. This quantity is also denoted as $i(F, A_j)$.

nodes.name: circumference of an annulus
nodes.statement: The total longitude variation $c_j$ of $A_j$ is defined as its \emph{circumference}. It equals to intersection number $i(F,\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ is any closed regular leaf of $F$ inside $A_j$. This quantity is also denoted as $i(G, A_j)$.

nodes.name: sliding deformation
nodes.statement: Let $(\Sigma_1; F_1, G_1)$, $(\Sigma_2; F_2, G_2)$ be two foliated dihedral surfaces with the same topological type and angle vector. They are said to \emph{be differed by a sliding deformation} if there exists a homeomorphism $J:\Sigma_1\to\Sigma_2$ preserving the label, such that $G_1=J^*G_2$ as measured foliation s on topological surfaces. In other words, a \emph{sliding deformation} of a foliated dihedral surface is changing the length of boundary segments while keeping the gluing pattern and widths of the bigons in strip decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Deformation preserving the longitude foliation: change boundary-segment lengths keeping gluing pattern and bigon widths.

nodes.name: Abelian differentials induce 1-parameter families of co-axial metrics
nodes.statement: It is observed in \cite{CWWX15} that an abelian differential $\omega$ induces a 1-parameter family of co-axial metrics, expressed by the developing map $$ D_\lambda(z) := \lambda \cdot \exp\left( \int_{z_0}^z \omega \right) := \lambda \cdot D_1(z),\quad \lambda\in\mathbb{R}_+ $$ as a multi-valued meromorphic function on $\Sigma-P$.
conclusions: induces a 1-parameter family of co-axial metrics

nodes.name: lambda-deformation
nodes.statement: We call changing the positive parameter the \emph{$\lambda$-deformation} of a co-axial surface.

nodes.name: Argument that lambda-deformation is sliding
nodes.statement: The $\lambda$-deformation changes the radial distance from the origin while keep the argument. Thus the longitude foliation is kept during the deformation, and so does the gluing pattern of strip decomposition. If $\abs{D_1(z)}=r(z)$, then the spherical distance from $D_1(z)$ to $0$ is $\int_0^{r(z)}\frac{2\mathrm{d}w}{1+w^2}=2\arctan r(z)$. Thus the spherical distance from $D_\lambda(z)$ to $0$ is $2\arctan\abs{D_\lambda(z)}=2\arctan(\lambda\cdot r(z))$.
nodes.statement_short: Direct computation: scaling preserves arguments and maps distance $2\arctan r$ to $2\arctan(\lambda r)$.

nodes.name: Arguments preserved, so longitude foliation and gluing patte
nodes.statement: The $\lambda$-deformation changes the radial distance from the origin while keep the argument. Thus the longitude foliation is kept during the deformation, and so does the gluing pattern of strip decomposition.
nodes.statement_short: Arguments preserved, so longitude foliation and gluing pattern are kept.

nodes.name: Compute the new spherical distance $2\arctan(\lambda r(z))$
nodes.statement: If $\abs{D_1(z)}=r(z)$, then the spherical distance from $D_1(z)$ to $0$ is $\int_0^{r(z)}\frac{2\mathrm{d}w}{1+w^2}=2\arctan r(z)$. Thus the spherical distance from $D_\lambda(z)$ to $0$ is $2\arctan\abs{D_\lambda(z)}=2\arctan(\lambda\cdot r(z))$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the new spherical distance $2\arctan(\lambda r(z))$.

nodes.name: lambda-deformation is a sliding deformation
nodes.statement: It is just a reassignment of the length of boundary segments of all bigons, thus a sliding deformation.
conclusions: a sliding deformation

nodes.name: Foliated moduli space distinguishes lambda-families
nodes.statement: The 1-forms $D^*_\lambda(\mathbf{i} z/\mathrm{d}z)$ on $\Sigma$ are the same for all $\lambda>0$. Thus one can not distinguish between the 1-parameter family of co-axial metrics that differ by $\lambda$-deformation based solely on 1-forms on the surface. These families of metrics are usually considered as one equivalent class in literature, such as in \cite{EGT14,CLY22axv}. Our modification on the transverse measure of $F$ allows us to distinguish this family by encoding more geometric information. Therefore, the moduli space of foliated surfaces is finer than the moduli space of 1-forms that induce co-axial metrics.
nodes.statement_short: Metrics differing by $\lambda$-deformation share the same 1-form; the modified measure of $F$ separates them.
nodes.label: rmk:equi_class

nodes.name: Limit of lambda-deformation
nodes.statement: We can consider the limit surface as $\lambda$ approaches 0. The distance from any points to the origin tends to $0$, except for $\infty$. This means that we lost information about all cone points, except for those mapped to $+\infty$. In terms of the strip decomposition, what remains is solely the number and width of bigons, and the gluing pattern for boundary segments that end at the south vertices. Based on this observation, we can assert that the limit of $\lambda$-deformation of a co-axial surface is a singular surface glued from several footballs along one of their vertices. In the summer of 2023, Zhiqiang Wei also achieved identical results for co-axial spheres. The number of footballs in the limit surface equals to the number of preimages $D^{-1}(\infty)$ on $\Sigma$. The case of $\lambda\to+\infty$ is similar. Such degenerated surfaces merit further investigation and are related to the boundary of moduli space.
nodes.statement_short: As $\lambda\to0$ a co-axial surface degenerates to footballs glued at a vertex.

nodes.name: split deformation
nodes.statement: For $p\in P\cap Q$ of cone angle $2k\pi, k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}$, the \emph{split deformation} slightly move it along $G$, so that the pole splits into $k$ poles which are smooth point on the surface, and the cone point becomes a zero of foliation with index $2-2k$. See Figure \ref{fig:split_pole} and the geometric description below. \begin{figure}[ht] \makebox[\textwidth][c]{\includegraphics[width=1.05\textwidth]{fig/SplitPole.png}} \caption{Splitting a pole of cone angle $6\pi$. Some leaves of $F$ is shown. Pay attention to the bold line that switches from a regular leaf to singular leaves.} \end{figure}
nodes.label: def:split

nodes.name: Cut-and-paste construction of splitting a pole
nodes.statement: Geometrically, this deformation is obtained by a cut-and-paste operation. First pick $k$ isometric longitude segments $v_1=p S_1, \cdots, v_k=p S_k$ from $p$, equally spaced by $2\pi$ angle. The length $\ell$ of these closed segments is small enough so that they contain no singularity other than $p$. Cutting the surface along $v_i$'s, one obtain a bordered surface with one boundary component. The cone point $p$ splits into $k$ boundary vertices $p_1, \cdots p_k$. Suppose the vertices are labeled as $S_1, p_1, S_2, p_2, \cdots S_k, p_k, S_1$ in counterclockwise order. Then glue $p_i S_i$ to $p_i S_{i+1}$ for all $i=1,\cdots, k$ (indices are modulo $k$). The foliation structure matches naturally, because the boundary are leaf segments of $G$ and perpendicular to leaves of $F$. All $S_i$ are glued to a common point, which is the new cone point of angle $2k\pi$, and each $p_i$ becomes a pole.
input: $p\in P\cap Q$ of cone angle $2k\pi, k\in\mathbb{Z}_{>1}$
nodes.statement_short: Cut along $k$ equally spaced short longitude segments at the pole and reglue shifted, turning the pole into a zero and $k$ smooth poles.

nodes.name: Choose $k$ equally spaced longitude segments of small length

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.19
nodes.statement: We call a critical leaf connecting zeros of $G$ \emph{vertical saddle connection}. Since $P$ is finite, there are finitely many vertical saddle connections in $\mathrm{Crit}(G)$. Let $\sigma$ be such a leaf connecting two zeros $p_1, p_2$, possibly the same. Now in the annulus decomposition of $(\Sigma;F,G)$, there exists an annulus $A=A(\sigma)$ passing through $\sigma$, and containing $p_1$ in one boundary component $C_1\subset \partial A$. It must not be a punctured disk. Otherwise the other end of $\sigma$ is the pole in that disk. There are finitely many leaves in $\mathrm{Crit}(G)$ intersecting $A$. These leaves, ending in singularities of $G$, must hit $C_1$. Then $C_1$ is divided into several open segments $I_1, \cdots, I_K$ by these intersections. Denote longitude variation of $I_j$ by $d_j=i(I_j,G)>0$. Let $t$ be a real number with $0<\abs{t}<\min\{d_1,\cdots,d_K\}$. Then a $t$-longitude twist along $A$ will break the vertical saddle connection $\sigma$, and not produce new vertical saddle connection. See Figure \ref{fig:twist_generic}. So we find a 1-parameter deformation of $(\Sigma;F,G)$ with fewer vertical saddle connections. Everything is unchanged outside the annulus $A$, and the local gluing data around cone points on $\partial A$ is fixed. So the angle vector and the type partition of the new surfaces are all the same. Finally, by induction, one can break all vertical saddle connections without changing the cone angles and the type partition. In addition, the absolute latitude of all cone points are fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Small twists along annuli through vertical saddle connections break them one at a time without creating new ones; induct.

nodes.statement: Follow the notations above. After twist deformation, the critical leaves from $p_1$ and $p_2$ in the direction of $\sigma$ mismatch at longitude variation $t$. nodes.name: Topological proof of Proposition 4.21
nodes.statement: Let $P=\{p_1, p_2\}$. Since $\pi_1(\Sigma-P)\cong \mathbb{Z}$, $\Sigma$ must be co-axial. Let $(\Sigma;F,G)$ be a foliated surface induced by developing map $D$ such that $\rho(\pi_1)\subset O(1)$. Recall that $Q=\pi D^{-1}\{N,S\}$. By Poincar\'{e}-Hopf\ formula (\ref{eq:PH}), $\sum \mathrm{Ind}(p) = 2(2-2g) = 4$. Since every cone point is a singularity of $G$, there is at most 2 zeros of $G$, or $\#(P-Q)\leq2$. If $p_1,p_2\in Q$, there is no other singularity, and $\mathrm{Crit}(G) = \emptyset$. Then $\Sigma$ must be some football $S_\theta$. If $p_1,p_2\in P-Q$, then $\theta_1,\theta_2\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $\rho(\pi_1)$ is trivial. We can always compose a $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ element so that $D(\pi^{-1}(p_1))=N$. So we only need to consider the case where $p_1\in Q$ and $p_2\in P-Q$. Then $\theta_2 = m \in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and $\rho(\pi_1)$ is trivial. So $D$ reduced to a univalent map, also denoted by $D$, directly from $\Sigma$ to $\mathbb{S}^2$. Let $X=D(p_2)\notin \{N,S\}$ and $B=D^{-1}(X,N)$. The developing map $D$ is a local homeomorphism\ outside cone points, so the restricted map $D:\Sigma-B \to \mathbb{S}^2-\{N,X\}$ is a covering map. Since $\theta_2 = m$, the degree of cover is $m$. Thus the reduced map $D:\Sigma\to\mathbb{S}^2$ is a $m$-sheet covering branched at $p_1,p_2$, and $\theta_1=\theta_2=m$. We obtained the desired result.

nodes.name: Spherical torus with one 4pi cone point and three strip decompositions
nodes.statement: A generic foliated surface in $\MsphDF{1}{1}{2}$ is glued by 2 bigons. The width $w_1, w_2$ of the two bigons satisfying $w_1+w_2=\pi$ so that the vertices of the bigons glued to a smooth point. The gluing pattern is shown in the left column of Figure \ref{fig:three_decomp}. However, there are two more choices of strip decomposition or foliation. The symmetry center of each bigon is the new pole of another foliation. The critical leaves of that longitude foliation on each bigon are also symmetric about its center. The middle and right column of Figure \ref{fig:three_decomp} shows how to cut the original bigons and glue to new ones. All blue and green arcs are geodesic segments. Let $x,x',x''$ be the length of the shorter boundary segment of bigons in each decomposition, and $w_1, w'_1, w''_1$ be the width of the bigon whose shorter boundary segment lies on the left. By spherical geometry, they satisfy the equations \[ \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \cos x' &= \sin x &\cos(w_1/2)\\ \cos x &= \sin x' &\sin(w'_1/2) \end{array}\right.,\quad \left\{ \begin{array}{lll} \cos x'' &= \sin x &\sin(w_1/2)\\ \cos x &= \sin x''&\cos(w''_1/2) \end{array}\right. .\] \hfill $\square$ \begin{figure}[hbt] \makebox[\textwidth][c]{\includegraphics[width=1.05\textwidth]{fig/TwoDecomp.png}} \caption{Three strip decomposition of a same spherical torus with one $4\pi$ cone point.} \end{figure}

nodes.name: Normalize a coset representative with $a>0$, $\arg b\in[0,\p
nodes.statement: \textbf{(Step 1).} We pick a representative for an element in $G_\Gamma/\mathrm{O}(2)$. If $\phi:z\mapsto \frac{az+b}{-\bar{b}z+\bar{a}} $, then \begin{align*} [\phi]:=\phi\cdot\mathrm{O}(2) &= \left\{\ z\mapsto \frac{a\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}z+b}{-\bar{b}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}z+\bar{a}},\quad z\mapsto \frac{a\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}+bz}{-\bar{b}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta}+\bar{a}z} \ \bigg\rvert\ \theta\in\mathbb{R} \ \right\} \\ & = \left\{\ z\mapsto \frac{a\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta/2}z+b\mathrm{e}^{-\mathbf{i}\theta/2}}{-\bar{b}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}\theta/2}z+\bar{a}\mathrm{e}^{-\mathbf{i}\theta/2}},\quad z\mapsto \frac{b\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}(\pi-\theta)/2}z+a\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}(\pi+\theta)/2}}{\bar{a}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}(\pi-\theta)/2}z-\bar{b}\mathrm{e}^{\mathbf{i}(\pi+\theta)/2}} \ \bigg\rvert\ \theta\in\mathbb{R} \ \right\}. \end{align*} Thus $\pm ab$ is the invariant of an element in $G_\Gamma/\mathrm{O}(2)$ in terms of $\mathrm{PSU}(2)$ representation. And $\phi\in\mathrm{O}(2)$ if and only if $ab=0$. So whenever $\phi\notin\mathrm{O}(2)$, we can choose a representative of $[\phi]$ such that $a>0$ and $\arg(b)\in[0,\pi)$.

nodes.statement: \textbf{(Step 3).} The rotation subgroup $\Gamma_0:=\Gamma\cap \mathrm{U}(1)$ must be $\mathbb{Z}_2$, so $\Gamma\cong K4$. $\Gamma_0$ can not be trivial. nodes.name: poles $q_1,\dots,q_m$ of a generic foliated surface
nodes.statement: Let $(\Sigma;F,G)$ be a generic foliated surface, with $m$ poles $\{q_1,\cdots, q_m\}$ of $F$.

nodes.name: bigons $B_1,\dots,B_b$ of the strip decomposition
nodes.statement: Assume its strip decomposition consists of $b$ bigons $\{B_1, \cdots, B_b\}$.

nodes.name: connection matrix
nodes.statement: The \emph{connection matrix} \textcolor{black}{$\mathbf{M}$} of $(\Sigma;F,G)$ is an $m \times b$ matrix with all entries in $\{0,1,2\}$, determined by the following: \begin{itemize} \item if both vertices of bigon $B_j$ are glued to one pole $q_i$, then $\mathbf{M}_{ij}:=2$ ; \item if vertices of $B_j$ are glued to different poles $q_i\neq q_{i'}$, then $\mathbf{M}_{ij}=\mathbf{M}_{i'j}:=1$; \item all the other entries are $0$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $m\times b$ matrix recording which poles each bigon's two vertices are glued to (entries 0,1,2).

nodes.name: cone-angle vector and width vector
nodes.statement: Let $\vec{C}:=(c_1, \cdots, c_m)^T$ be the column vector recording cone angles at poles $q_i$ on $\Sigma$, and $\vec{W}:=(w_1, \cdots, w_b)^T$ be the vector recording widths of $B_j$.

nodes.name: Path-connectedness of the connection matrix
nodes.statement: For generic $(\Sigma;F,G)$, its connection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is path-connected in the following sense: for any two non-zero elements $\mathbf{M}_{ij}, \mathbf{M}_{kl}$, there exists a finite sequence $(i_0,j_0), (i_1,j_1), \cdots, (i_N, j_N)$ such that \begin{itemize} \item $(i_0,j_0)=(i,j), (i_N, j_N)=(k,l)$; \item $(i_{t-1},j_{t-1}), (i_{t},j_{t})$ have exactly one same component for all $t=1,\cdots,N$; \item all entries $\mathbf{M}_{(i_{t},j_{t})}$ are non-zero. \end{itemize}
conclusions: its connection matrix $\mathbf{M}$ is path-connected

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.8
nodes.statement: We first prove the statement for $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$, then project it to $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$. \textbf{(Step 1).} By Corollary \ref{cor:low_dim}, to count the real parameters for $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$, we only need to consider generic foliated surfaces. Let $(\Sigma;F,G)\in \mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$ be a generic foliated surface. Suppose that there are $b$ bigons in the strip decomposition, and $m\geq0$ extra poles other than the cone points. The strip decomposition can be viewed as a cell decomposition of $\Sigma$, and each bigon is a topological quadrilateral. By computing the Euler characteristic we have \[ 2-2g = (n_E + n_O + n_N + m) - 2b + b. \] So $b = m+n+(2g-2) $. Every zero of even index provides one parameter, namely its absolute latitude. Every zero of odd index must lie on the equatorial net (Definition \ref{def:singular_info}), not providing new parameter. The widths of the $b$ bigons are the other real parameters, constrained by $n_N+m$ linear equations $\vec{C}=\mathbf{M} \vec{W}$, where $\mathbf{M}$ is the $(n_N+m)\times b$ connection matrix. By Proposition \ref{prop:rank}, for strict dihedral surface, $\mathbf{M}$ is full-rank. Then the dimension of the solution space of the width vector $\vec{W}$ is \[ b - \mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{M}) = \big(m+n+(2g-2)\big) - \big( n_N+m \big) = n - n_N + 2g-2. \] Together with the parameters from the zeros of even index, the total dimension is \[ n_E + (n - n_N + 2g-2) = 2 n_E + n_O + 2g-2. \] \textbf{(Step 2).} By Proposition \ref{prop:id_SDhd}, the fibers of $p_T:\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T}) \to \mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$ is always finite, so the projection $p_T$ preserves dimension. Since generic foliated surfaces form the top-dimensional subset of $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$ by Corollary \ref{cor:low_dim}, the real dimension of $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$ is the same as $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^D(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$.

For each bigon $B_j$ in the strip decomposition, pick an interior segment $e_j$ connecting the two boundary marked points, and orient it along $F$. Each $B_j$ is cut into two half-pieces by $e_j$, and all half-pieces glued to the same pole $q_l$ form a topological disk $d_l$. The zeros of $F$, the segments $\{ e_j \}_{j=1}^{b}$, and the disks $\{d_l\}_{l=1}^{m}$ form a cell decomposition of $\Sigma$. When all $\theta_i\in\mathbb{Z}$, the closed loops around every cone point have trivial monodromy. So we can further replace $H_1(\Sigma-P)$ with $H_1(\Sigma)$. Then the oriented segments $\{e_j\}$ form a basis of the chain group $C_1(\Sigma)$. The effect on the monodromy of moving along $e_j$ is a $2\pi w_j$-rotation. For $\gamma\in H_1(\Sigma)$, if $\rho(\gamma)=z \mapsto e^{2\pi\mathbf{i} \psi} \in \mathrm{U}(1)$, define $(\ln\rho)(\gamma):=\psi\in[0,1)$. Then we have \[\ln\rho \begin{pmatrix} a_1 \\ \vdots \\ a_{2g} \end{pmatrix} \equiv X \begin{pmatrix} w_1 \\ \vdots \\ w_b \end{pmatrix} \quad (\text{mod } \mathbb{Z}). \] On the other hand, since $F$ is orientable, the connection matrix contains no entry 2, and we can improve it with signature. As in the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:rank}.(2), define $\mathbf{M}_{ij}=+1$ if $B_j$ is glued to pole $q_i$ that lies on the left of $F$, and define $\mathbf{M}_{ij}=-1$ if $q_i$ lies on the right of $F$. Then the total sum of each column in this $\mathbf{M}$ is 0. The boundary chain of each disk $d_l$ consists of segments with same signature. So we can orient them properly so that \[\begin{pmatrix} \partial d_1 \\ \vdots \\ \partial d_m \end{pmatrix} = \mathbf{M} \begin{pmatrix} e_1 \\ \vdots \\ e_b \end{pmatrix}, \] where $\partial:C_2(\Sigma) \to C_1(\Sigma)$ is the boundary operator. Since $a_1,\cdots,a_{2g}$ generates $H_1(\Sigma)$, they must be linearly independent at chain level. Then rows of $X$ are linearly independent. However, each row of $\mathbf{M}$ gives a boundary chain. So each row of $X$ is linearly independent of all rows in $\mathbf{M}$. \medskip \textbf{(Step 2).} Suppose $(\Sigma;F,G)$ has trivial monodromy and $\vec{W}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^b$ is the width vector. By Proposition \ref{prop:rank}, $\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{M}) = m-1$. Let $\boldsymbol{M}_1,\cdots,\boldsymbol{M}_{m-1}$ be $(m-1)$ linearly independent rows of $\mathbf{M}$, and $\boldsymbol{X}_1,\cdots,\boldsymbol{X}_{2g}$ be the rows of $X$. If these rows are linearly dependent, there exists $\lambda_1,\cdots,\lambda_{m-1},\mu_1,\cdots,\mu_{2g}$ such that $$ \lambda_1 \boldsymbol{M}_1 + \cdots + \lambda_{m-1} \boldsymbol{M}_{m-1} = \mu_1 \boldsymbol{X}_1 + \cdots + \mu_{2g} \boldsymbol{X}_{2g}. $$ and at least one $\lambda_i$ and $\mu_j$ is non-zero. Applying this equation on the basis $\left( e_1, \cdots, e_b \right)^T$, the left side becomes a linear combination of $\partial d_1,\cdots,\partial d_m$, which must be exact. And the right side becomes a linear combination of the homology basis $a_1,\cdots,a_{2g}$, which can not be exact. Then both sides are zero. Since $\boldsymbol{X}_j$'s are linearly independent, all $\mu_j$ is zero, a contradiction. Thus $$\mathrm{rank}\begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{M} \\ X \end{pmatrix} \geq m-1+2g$$ and the solution space of (\ref{eq:width_constrain_mond}) has dimension $\leq b-(m-1+2g) < b-(m-1)$. The choices for $\vec{C}_0\in\mathbb{Z}_+^m$ and $\vec{A}\in\mathbb{Z}^{2g}$ are finite because $0<w_i\leq\max\{\theta_1,\cdots,\theta_n, 2\pi\}$. So the solution space for width vector is a finite union of subsets with dimension strictly smaller than $b-(m-1)= b-\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{M})$. So generic foliated surfaces with trivial monodromy form a lower dimensional subset in $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$ \medskip \textbf{(Step 3).} By Lemma \ref{prop:id_CoAx}.(2), $p_T$ is injective on the subset of generic foliated surfaces with non-trivial monodromy. If these rows are linearly dependent, there exists $\lambda_1,\cdots,\lambda_{m-1},\mu_1,\cdots,\mu_{2g}$ such that $$ \lambda_1 \boldsymbol{M}_1 + \cdots + \lambda_{m-1} \boldsymbol{M}_{m-1} = \mu_1 \boldsymbol{X}_1 + \cdots + \mu_{2g} \boldsymbol{X}_{2g}. $$ and at least one $\lambda_i$ and $\mu_j$ is non-zero. Applying this equation on the basis $\left( e_1, \cdots, e_b \right)^T$, the left side becomes a linear combination of $\partial d_1,\cdots,\partial d_m$, which must be exact. And the right side becomes a linear combination of the homology basis $a_1,\cdots,a_{2g}$, which can not be exact. Then both sides are zero. Since $\boldsymbol{X}_j$'s are linearly independent, all $\mu_j$ is zero, a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: A dependency between rows would equate exact and non-exact chains: contradiction.

nodes.statement_short: Combined rank $\ge m-1+2g$.

So the solution space for width vector is a finite union of subsets with dimension strictly smaller than $b-(m-1)= b-\mathrm{rank}(\mathbf{M})$. nodes.name: Project via injective $p_T$ on nontrivial monodromy
nodes.statement: \textbf{(Step 3).} By Lemma \ref{prop:id_CoAx}.(2), $p_T$ is injective on the subset of generic foliated surfaces with non-trivial monodromy. We have shown that in $\mathcal{M}sphF_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$, generic foliated surfaces with trivial monodromy form a lower dimensional subset, and non-generic foliated surfaces already form a lower dimensional subset. Since $p_T$ does not increase the dimension, the image of generic surfaces with non-trivial monodromy must form the top dimensional subset in $\mathcal{M}sph_{g,n}^C(\vec{\theta};\vec{T})$.
